title: Deploy Container
summary: Adversaries deploy containers to run code and to sidestep controls that watch for malicious processes on a host. The deployment may use a malicious image that already contains the payload, or a benign public image that downloads and executes code at start up, which keeps the image itself unremarkable. Attackers also deliberately deploy containers configured without the network policies, resource limits, or user restrictions that normally apply, so they obtain a permissive environment inside an otherwise defended cluster. In Kubernetes, deployment happens through the API using workloads such as pods, ReplicaSets, or DaemonSets, and a DaemonSet in particular places a container on many nodes at once. Scheduling a privileged container onto a chosen node is a common precursor to an escape attempt. Detection draws on Kubernetes audit logs for create operations, image registry records, and runtime telemetry showing container processes that do not match the expected workload.

beginner.definition: Deploying a container means starting a new container from an image. An image is a packaged copy of an application and its files. An attacker can start their own container in order to run code. In many logs this looks like ordinary platform activity.
beginner.whyItMatters: Containers are quick to start, so an attacker can work without touching the host directly. A container that ignores your normal limits may bypass controls you rely on. It can also run software that your endpoint tools never inspect. If deployment is not logged and reviewed, you lose the first clue.
howItWorks: The attacker needs access to the platform, usually a stolen key or account.
They choose an image, either one they built themselves or a normal public image.
They send a start request to the platform, or use a web dashboard instead.
The platform schedules the container onto a node and starts it running.
The container may download more code at start up, so the image itself stays clean.
Some deployments skip normal limits, leaving the container with more access than intended.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel where guests book a room online and never speak to anyone at the desk. A visitor books a room, then brings their own furniture, their own lock, and their own rules for the floor. Staff see a normal booking in the system and nothing unusual at the desk. Only when somebody inspects the room do they find equipment that does not belong to the hotel. The booking record existed long before anyone looked inside.
takeaways: Running a container is a way to execute code while staying off the host.
A clean public image can still download and run malicious code at start up.
Deployments that ignore normal limits deserve immediate attention.

objectives: Explain why an adversary would deploy a container rather than run code on a host.
Describe how a benign base image can be used to run malicious code at runtime.
Identify Kubernetes workload types that spread a container across many nodes.
Explain how deployment without normal restrictions weakens existing defences.
State which audit records show container creation in a cluster.
